title: File storage for tables and artifacts
request: Tables and artifacts do not belong in the database. Put uploaded files, cleaned Parquet tables and exports behind one file storage (a local folder now, S3-compatible later), record each file with its key, size, SHA-256 and content type, and check the hash when a stage loads data.
spec: dclab_rnd/storage/files.py with put, open, delete and exists; a local-folder implementation and an S3-compatible one (boto3 imported lazily); file records in the database; the sanitised-name and size-limit rules kept; never a credential in a record. Done when a project's data can be read after the workspace folder is moved and the hash is checked on read.
plan: Map how data files are stored and read today (an explore agent): project and draft documents hold bare file names, and in PostgreSQL mode the workspace id is the folder's absolute path, so moving the folder would lose every project.
Give a workspace folder a stable identity: a .dclab_workspace marker holding the old key (the path), so existing workspaces keep their id and a moved folder stays the same workspace.
Write files.py: keys relative to the workspace folder, LocalFiles and S3Files, records in a stored_file table (migration 0008) or .dclab_files.json.

Record project data, draft uploads and cleaned tables, and the intern's exports; make every read of a project's table go through data_path, which checks the recorded SHA-256 (the engine, the Solution routes, the intern's tools).
Write tests, including the moved-folder test on PostgreSQL; run the gate and the reviewer; fix; commit.

decisions.decision: The workspace marker stores the folder's old path as its key.
decisions.why: Existing PostgreSQL workspaces were keyed by that path; keeping it as the marker's content means no migration of ids, while a moved folder carries its identity with it.

decisions.decision: Every read of a project's table checks the recorded hash, and a changed table is a 409, never modelled.
decisions.why: A file that changed on disk after it was recorded would otherwise go straight into a model and silently change the results.

decisions.decision: S3 credentials come only from boto3's default chain; records hold no bucket URL or credential.
decisions.why: A file record is shown and copied; it must never carry a secret.

decisions.decision: The intern's export returns keys, not absolute paths.
decisions.why: An absolute path leaks the machine's layout and means nothing to another instance or a bucket.

change: New dclab_rnd/storage/files.py (put, open, path, exists, delete, key_of; LocalFiles, S3Files; JsonRecords and PgRecords), migration 0008 stored_file, db.workspace_for with the .dclab_workspace marker used by every open_* store. studio/data.py gained data_path (hash-checked) and attach_data records the new file and deletes old files with their records; the engine, the server's load_frame, the draft pipeline, the draft and project delete routes and the intern's tools use it. tests/test_file_storage.py.

findings.defect: In PostgreSQL mode a workspace whose folder was moved lost every project.
findings.scenario: A workspace folder is moved to another disk and the server started on the new path: the workspace id was derived from the folder's absolute path, so open_stores made a new, empty workspace and projects.get raised KeyError for every old id.
findings.cause: The folder's path was the workspace's only identity.
findings.fix: The folder carries its identity in a .dclab_workspace marker (holding the old path, so existing workspaces keep their id); every store opener reads it through workspace_for.
findings.impact: Moving a workspace folder to another disk in PostgreSQL mode made every project vanish from the product: the server opened a new, empty workspace and every old project id raised, though all the rows were still in the database.
findings.open: A copied workspace folder now shares the original's PostgreSQL rows: a project made in the copy shows in the original with a missing file, and deleting it in one removes it from both.

findings.defect: Attaching a table whose name starts with '-' deleted the project's current table and then failed, leaving the project pointing at a missing file.
findings.scenario: Attach good.csv, then attach -sales.csv: safe_name keeps the leading '-', but the key rule demanded a letter or digit first; attach_data had already deleted every other file in data/, so put raised FileError (a ValueError, not a DataError), the upload returned 500, the project still named good.csv, and every later stage failed with 'missing'. A store folder with a space in its name, a draft asset named -sales, or a storage error in put took the same path.
findings.cause: The key rule was stricter than the upload's name rule, and attach_data deleted the old files before storing the new one.
findings.fix: A key part is any name without a separator or NUL (refusing empty, '.', '..' and a leading '/'); attach_data stores the new file first and deletes the old ones only after it succeeds; any storage error becomes a DataError and leaves the project untouched; project and draft deletes forget their records best effort so deletion always works.
findings.impact: A user who uploaded a file whose name starts with '-' lost the project's current table: the upload returned 500, the project still pointed at the deleted file, and every later stage failed with 'missing' until data was attached again.
alternatives: Make safe_name strip a leading '-': set aside, because a folder name with a space or a storage error took the same path; the key rule now accepts every name safe_name keeps, and the new file is stored before the old one is deleted.
findings.open: When a person re-uploads under the current table's own name, the upload route overwrites that file before attach_data runs, so a failed attach still loses it; this predates 9.3.

findings.defect: A storage error while recording a draft upload left the asset in its first status for ever.
findings.scenario: With DCLAB_FILES_URL=s3://... and no credentials, botocore raises NoCredentialsError (not an OSError) from _record, which ran before the try that marks an asset failed; the exception escaped run(), no 'failed' event was sent and the Home agent was never told.
findings.cause: _record caught only ValueError and OSError and ran outside the failure handling.
findings.fix: _record is best effort and catches any Exception.
findings.impact: With S3 configured but no credentials, an upload stayed in its first status for ever: no 'failed' event, the Home agent never told, and the user waiting on data that would never be ready.
alternatives: Move the first _record inside the try that marks an asset failed: also offered; making _record best effort, as its docstring already said it was, keeps a recording failure from ever stopping the pipeline.

findings.defect: A folder inside the workspace that is a symbolic link made key_of raise a plain ValueError.
findings.scenario: A project folder moved to another disk and linked back resolves outside the workspace root; relative_to raises ValueError, so load_frame returned 500 instead of 409 and attach_data took the data-loss path of F1.
findings.cause: key_of resolved both the path and the root, following the link out of the root.
findings.fix: key_of uses abspath on both sides without resolving links and raises FileError outside the root; data_path builds the storage inside its try.
findings.impact: A workspace whose project folder was linked in from another disk got a 500 instead of a 409 when reading data, and attaching a new table there took the data-loss path of F1.

findings.defect: A rewrite of a table with the same size and a restored modification time passed the hash check.
findings.scenario: put 'a,b / 1,2', overwrite with 'a,b / 9,9', restore the mtime (cp -p, touch -r, a tar restore, or a coarse filesystem clock): path() returned the changed bytes as verified.
findings.cause: The SHA-256 cache was keyed by path, size and mtime only.
findings.fix: The cache key also holds the inode and the change time, which utime cannot set.
findings.impact: A table rewritten with the same size and its old modification time (cp -p, a tar restore) passed the hash check, so changed data would reach a model as if it were the recorded table and every later score would describe data no record names.

findings.defect: The file records' JSON store was safe in one process only.
findings.scenario: The server and a standalone MCP server share one records file; two writes at once both used the fixed temp name .dclab_files.tmp, so one os.replace raised FileNotFoundError after the old files were deleted, or the last writer silently dropped a record.
findings.cause: A process-local lock and a fixed temporary file name.
findings.fix: Writes go through a unique mkstemp file in the same folder under an fcntl lock on a lock file plus the process lock; reads stay lock-free because os.replace is atomic.
findings.test: Covered by the file-storage tests on both backends.
findings.impact: With the server and a standalone MCP server writing file records at once, one write could fail after the old files were deleted, or a record could silently vanish, leaving a table on disk with nothing to check it against.

findings.defect: S3Files read a whole object into memory before checking the size limit.
findings.scenario: A large or hostile object in the bucket is fully buffered before MAX_BYTES is compared.
findings.cause: The size check came after read().
findings.fix: Refuse when ContentLength exceeds MAX_BYTES before reading, and read at most MAX_BYTES plus one byte.
findings.test: The S3 size refusal test in tests/test_file_storage.py.
findings.impact: A large or hostile object in the bucket was read whole into memory before the size check, so one oversized file could exhaust the server's memory for every user.
alternatives: Stream the object into the partial file and stop at the limit: offered by the reviewer; checking the size header and capping the read is the smaller change.

findings.defect: The new 'could not be stored' error carried the raw database error to the page.
findings.scenario: With DCLAB_DATABASE_URL set and the database down, an upload's 400 body read '(psycopg.OperationalError) connection failed: connection to server at host, port ...', and with a wrong password it named the database user.
findings.cause: The fix for F1 wrapped any storage exception as DataError(f'...{exc}').
findings.fix: The message is the FileError's own text, or only the exception's type for any other error, as the database health check already does.
findings.test: Re-checked by the reviewer; the storage-failure test asserts the message.
findings.impact: With the database down or a wrong password, an upload's error put the database host, port and user on the page: parts of a connection string, which must never reach a response.

outcome: Done after two review rounds: tables and artifacts behind one file storage (folder or S3), each recorded with its SHA-256 and checked on every read of a project's table; a moved workspace folder keeps its projects in PostgreSQL. Left open and written down: draft reads and connector downloads are recorded but not checked on read, HTTP exports are built in memory, and a copied workspace folder shares the original's PostgreSQL rows.
lessons: When two rules decide the same name (upload sanitising and storage keys), make one accept everything the other produces, or the gap becomes data loss.
Store the new file before deleting the old one; any failure in between must leave the previous state intact.
A hash cache keyed by mtime can be fooled; include values a user cannot set back, such as the inode and change time.
Wrapping an exception's text into a user message can leak connection details; name the type instead.
risks: A workspace whose only identity is its folder path loses its projects in the database when the folder moves.
Deleting the old table before the new one is stored turns any storage error into data loss.
Two rules that decide the same name (upload sanitising and storage keys) can disagree and make some uploads fail midway.
A file that changed on disk after it was recorded goes straight into a model unless every read checks the hash.
A file record or an error message could carry an S3 credential, a bucket URL or database connection details.
